def: Faraday's laws state that an EMF is induced in a circuit whenever the magnetic flux linked with it changes, and the induced EMF is proportional to the rate of change of that flux.
points: First law: EMF is induced only when flux through a circuit changes, and lasts only as long as the change continues.
Second law: induced EMF e = -N d(phi)/dt, where N is number of turns and phi is flux through one turn.
The negative sign shows the induced EMF opposes the change producing it (Lenz's law).
Flux can change by moving a magnet, changing current in a nearby coil, or changing the area/orientation of the coil.
These laws were discovered experimentally by moving magnets near coils and observing induced current.
They explain working of generators, transformers, and induction-based sensors.

diagram.draw: Draw a bar magnet being pushed towards a coil connected to a galvanometer. Show flux lines passing through the coil with arrows. Label the induced current direction in the coil and the galvanometer deflection.

example: A coil of 500 turns has flux change from 2e-3 Wb to 6e-3 Wb in 0.1 s. EMF = 500 x (4e-3/0.1) = 20 V.
tip: State both laws separately in words, then write the formula with the negative sign — examiners check for the sign explanation.

def: Lenz's law states that the induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it, consistent with conservation of energy.
points: The opposing nature of induced current is shown by the negative sign in Faraday's equation.
To change the flux against this opposition, external work must be done — this work becomes the electrical energy in the circuit.
Example: pushing a magnet into a coil induces a current whose field repels the magnet, so you must push harder.
If induced current instead helped the change, flux would grow on its own — a free energy source, which is impossible.
Lenz's law gives the direction of induced current and also justifies the law physically through energy conservation.
It is essential for predicting current direction in every electromagnetic induction (EMI) problem.
formula: Direction of induced current always opposes the change in flux (shown by - sign in e = -N dphi/dt)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Flux through coil increases"] --> B["Induced current opposes increase"]
  B --> C["Induced magnetic field opposes external magnet"]
  C --> D["Extra work needed matches electrical energy produced"]

example: When the north pole of a magnet is pushed into a coil, the induced current flows so as to create a north pole facing the magnet, repelling it.
tip: Use the right-hand rule to find induced current direction after applying Lenz's law for full marks in direction-based questions.

def: Motional EMF is the EMF induced in a conductor moving through a magnetic field, causing the circuit's area (and flux) to change with time.
points: Consider a straight rod of length L moving with velocity v perpendicular to field B.
The free charges in the rod experience magnetic force F = qv x B, pushing them to one end.
This creates a potential difference across the rod, which is the motional EMF.
At steady state, EMF e = B L v (rod, field and velocity all mutually perpendicular).
This same result can also be derived from rate of change of flux as the rod sweeps area.
Motional EMF explains the basic working of generators where a coil moves or rotates in a magnetic field.

diagram.draw: Draw two parallel horizontal rails with a rod sliding across them, moving to the right with velocity v. Draw the magnetic field B pointing into the page with crosses. Show the induced EMF/current direction in the rod using the right-hand rule, label L as the rod length.

example: A rod of length 0.5 m moves at 4 m/s perpendicular to a field of 0.2 T. EMF = 0.2 x 0.5 x 4 = 0.4 V.
tip: Derive the formula using F = qv x B pushing charges to one end — examiners like seeing this derivation, not just the formula.

def: Self inductance is the property of a coil by which a changing current in itself induces an EMF in it; mutual inductance is the property by which a changing current in one coil induces an EMF in a neighbouring coil.
points: Self-induced EMF: e = -L dI/dt, where L is self inductance of the coil.
For a long solenoid, L = mu0 n^2 A l, depending only on geometry and medium.
Mutual induced EMF in coil 2 due to changing current in coil 1: e2 = -M dI1/dt.
M depends on turns, geometry, separation and relative orientation of the two coils.
Self inductance opposes any change of current, similar to inertia opposing change of velocity.
Mutual inductance is the basis of energy transfer between coupled coils, as in a transformer.
formula: e = -L dI/dt     e2 = -M dI1/dt     Solenoid: L = mu0 n^2 A l

diagram.draw: Draw two coils side by side, wound close together (coil 1 and coil 2). Connect coil 1 to a battery and switch; connect coil 2 to a galvanometer. Show flux lines from coil 1 passing through coil 2, and label the mutual inductance M.

example: A solenoid with n=1000 turns/m, A=0.001 m^2, l=0.5 m has L = 4 pi x10^-7 x (1000)^2 x 0.001 x 0.5 ≈ 6.28 x 10^-4 H.
tip: Write both self and mutual EMF formulas together and clearly distinguish single-coil vs two-coil effects.

def: The energy stored in an inductor is the work done to establish the current against its back-EMF, stored as magnetic potential energy in its field.
points: When current grows from 0 to I in an inductor, work is done against the back-EMF e = -L dI/dt.
This work gets stored as magnetic field energy, U = (1/2) L I^2.
This formula is similar to (1/2) C V^2 for a capacitor and (1/2) m v^2 for a moving mass.
The energy can be released back when current (and field) decreases, sometimes producing a spark.
This explains the voltage spike seen when switching off a circuit containing an inductor (like a relay coil).
Understanding this is important for designing inductors in power supplies and filters.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Current increases in inductor"] --> B["Work done against back EMF"]
  B --> C["Energy stored as magnetic field"]
  C --> D["U = half L I squared"]

example: An inductor of L = 2 H carries current I = 3 A. Energy stored U = 0.5 x 2 x 9 = 9 J.
tip: Mention the analogy with capacitor energy and kinetic energy formulas — comparing them is a common conceptual mark.

def: Eddy currents are closed loops of induced current that circulate inside a bulk conductor when it experiences a changing magnetic flux.
points: Eddy currents arise from the same Faraday-Lenz principle, but flow in loops within solid metal rather than in wires.
By Lenz's law, these currents oppose the change in flux causing them.
They dissipate energy as heat due to the resistance of the material — a loss in transformers and motors.
Laminating the core (thin insulated sheets) increases resistance to eddy currents, reducing this loss.
Useful applications: electromagnetic braking in trains, induction furnaces, speedometers, metal detectors.
Eddy current strength depends on rate of flux change, conductivity, and size of the conducting body.
formula: Eddy current power loss (proportional to) (rate of flux change)^2 and conductivity

diagram.draw: Draw a solid metal plate with a changing magnetic field (shown by field lines with an arrow indicating increasing strength) passing through it. Draw small circular loops (eddy currents) inside the plate opposing the change, with arrows showing their circulation direction.

example: In electromagnetic braking, a metal disc moving through a magnetic field develops eddy currents that oppose its motion, slowing the disc without any physical contact.
tip: Give at least one useful application (braking/induction furnace) and one harmful effect (transformer core heating) with the laminated-core solution, for full marks.
